title: Senate inquiry urges sweeping reforms to Triple Zero outage crises
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Control of a vital Triple Zero (000) function should be removed from Telstra and nationalised to avoid further crises, a Senate inquiry has recommended.

The inquiry was prompted by last year's Optus outage, which has been linked to two deaths, and was expanded to cover new problems with other major telcos and mobile devices that have shaken public confidence.

The report was handed down this afternoon and made 11 recommendations to overhaul the system, including:

Mandating domestic roaming,

Introducing minimum performance and reliability standards with automatic compensation for those impacted by outages, and

Creating the ability for the public to text Triple Zero in an emergency.

Telstra's national outage Government agencies and academics recently warned Telstra it was vulnerable to the type of error that caused this week's national outage.

The inquiry was chaired by Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young, but the report was supported by Coalition and Labor committee members.

"Australian telcos are now on notice. This is the end of the era of self-regulation," Senator Hanson-Young said.

"After months of work, this report recommends essential measures the government must enact if they want to end Australia's telco crisis."

The committee has called for a new national authority to be created and take over responsibility for the Emergency Call Person operations.

That role is currently performed by Telstra and involves answering calls to Triple Zero and transferring them to local emergency services.

The inquiry was chaired by Senator Sarah Hanson-Young. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"Triple Zero is an essential service. It is often a matter of life or death for people. We can no longer allow it to be left to private companies," Senator Hanson-Young said.

Advocates have also pushed for domestic roaming, which would allow customers to access another company's network if their telco's service was unavailable.

However, Telstra previously told the ABC that roaming could cause problems during a major outage by placing "extraordinary demand" on remaining networks.

More Optus network Triple Zero failures A woman was unable to call Triple Zero after robbers broke into her home while she was in the bedroom.

The ACCC rejected the idea in 2017 after finding it would reduce incentives for telcos to invest in their networks, but the consumer watchdog is now reconsidering it as part of a new inquiry.

There is also a push to make it possible for people in an emergency to send a text message requesting help, in addition to voice calls.

A pilot is currently being established, which would test whether technology could make this possible.

The committee has also called for an independent review of the telco watchdog, the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), to ensure its powers, resourcing and regulatory approach are up to scratch for the Triple Zero system.

The regulator should be given the power to compel evidence from telcos during investigations and enforcement, it said.

title: 'Like Dante's Inferno': Residents angry at lack of fire ban despite dire forecast
text:
Residents east of Hobart have questioned why a total fire ban was not imposed over the weekend, after they spent the evening fearing an ember attack from a nearby blaze.

A bushfire erupted at Seven Mile Beach, about 15 kilometres east of Hobart, on Sunday amid hot and windy conditions, before being brought under control by the Tasmania Fire Service (TFS) on Sunday night.

Smoke from the Seven Mile Beach bushfire, seen from Dodges Ferry, on Sunday. (ABC News: Jo Spargo)

Gusts of up to 100 kilometres per hour were recorded near Hobart on Sunday, with the temperature peaking at 27.1 degrees Celsius.

The only separation between the blaze and the residential communities of Lewisham and Dodges Ferry was a body of water about 400 metres wide, with smoke billowing towards houses.

Lewisham resident Suzy Lebasi said it was "like Dante's Inferno over on the other shore" with "horrendous smoke" blowing over Dodges Ferry in particular.

"We were all on alert for a possible ember blowing and burning our houses down, so it was not a happy afternoon," Ms Lebasi said.

A burn-off had been registered in the area, however, the fire service has not declared the cause of the bushfire. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Kylie Reardon, who also lives in Lewisham, said most residents in the suburbs "would have been sleeping with one eye open last night" due to the fire.

Dodges Ferry resident Steve Lord said the smoke became so strong he could not see Lewisham, while former TFS commissioner Carmel Torenius said some residents had embers "falling around their house".

Dodges Ferry resident Steve Lord says the smoke obscured Lewisham. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The fire conditions had been forecast, with the TFS holding a press conference on Friday "strongly discouraging" residents preparing registered burns "from continuing with those activities".

The ABC put questions to the TFS on the rules governing the declaration of a total fire ban.

In response, the fire service said: "Permit restrictions are generally implemented as a seasonal administrative public safety measure and to provide situational awareness of planned burning activities across the landscape."

"They are not normally applied and removed in response to individual weather events in the same manner as a Total Fire Ban (TFB)."

The TFS said with regard to Sunday's fire activity, it "remains very early in the fire season and, while there was some fire activity, the overall area impacted was relatively limited".

"Regional preparedness arrangements were activated, and resources were assembled and positioned appropriately to manage the prevailing risk."

The fire was still smouldering on Monday. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Burn-off takes place despite warnings

A burn-off was registered for private land at Seven Mile Beach over the weekend, which some residents saw taking place in the two days preceding the bushfire.

The TFS is still investigating the cause of the bushfire at Seven Mile Beach.

"Fire investigators will be on scene today to start their investigations into the cause of the fire," a TFS spokesperson said.

"Fire investigations can be complex, and will take time.

"There is development occurring in the vicinity of the Seven Mile Beach fire, but it is too early to comment on the land management activities being used and whether this caused, or contributed to, the fire."

The forecast fire danger rating released on Friday showed pockets of extreme and high fire danger for Sunday. (Supplied: Tasmania Fire Service)

Ms Lebasi said she felt a total fire ban should have been imposed over the weekend, given the strong winds forecast across the area.

"The circumstances were pretty much the same as the fire … that took off and then wiped out Dunalley [in 2013] — that's what it looked like yesterday," she said.

Ms Reardon said that while it was still only spring, it was clear that fire preparedness conversations needed to take place "at a community level".

"People who are lighting fires on their property need to be thinking about the forecast on the day that they light it but also the days and possibly weeks after that," she said.

Improper burn-offs a 'real concern' for firefighters

TFS deputy regional chief John Holloway said about 60 fires were reported on Sunday, with a large number of them connected to burn-offs by people who "weren't prepared for the weather".

"That's a real concern for us going into the summer … you really need to be keeping an eye on the weather, keeping an eye on the warnings we're putting out," Mr Holloway said.

" They are responsible for the damage that those fires can do, so if you burn your neighbour's fence down, their house down — or worse — that's your responsibility. "

He said that while there were currently no "formal permits" required for burn-offs, people still needed to pay attention to weather conditions and warnings.

Local resident and former TFS commissioner Carmel Torenius says residents need to be vigilant. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Mr Holloway said "just one ember" could start a fire if the conditions were dry enough; however, the TFS was not expecting anything to impact the Dodges Ferry community on Monday, except smoke.

Ms Torenius said residents would have to "be vigilant" this summer, as it was already very dry across the south-east region.

Two bushfires that burned at Colebrook in the state's southern midlands on Sunday have also been brought under control.

The TFS issued a warning on Friday about the elevated fire risk expected over the weekend due to the forecast weather conditions.

title: Breaking: Cindy Crawford's son dies aged 27
text:
Tell us about your experience.

American supermodel Cindy Crawford's son, Presley Gerber, has died aged 27.

Gerber's death was listed on the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner portal as having occurred at a rehab facility on Sunday, local time.

Several US media outlets also reported that a representative of the family had confirmed the death and had asked for the family's privacy to be respected.

The 27-year-old was the only son of Crawford and her businessman husband, Rande Gerber, and the older brother of model-actor Kaia Gerber.

Gerber's Instagram profile, where he had previously documented his battle with mental health, was flowing with tributes on Monday.

title: Country footballer wins premiership with Echuca despite brain cancer
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Echuca footballer Aiden "AJ" Mills has celebrated a premiership a year after he was denied a permit to play finals while undergoing treatment for brain cancer.

Mills played for the Murray Bombers' senior side in the Goulburn Valley Football League grand final against Shepparton yesterday, kicking two goals, including one on the final siren.

Echuca won the match by 81 points, finishing 21.15 (141) to Shepparton 8.12 (60).

Mills was moved forward late in the final quarter, with coach Troy Murphy hoping he could kick a goal.

"He took a big mark with about five minutes to go and kicked the goal," Murphy said.

" I think everyone in the ground had tears in their eyes and were just absolutely ecstatic that he'd done it. "

Mills then kicked another goal on the final siren.

"It was just the icing on the cake. It was amazing," Murphy said.

Denied a chance

Mills was diagnosed with brain cancer during last year's football season and underwent surgery and treatment.

AJ Mills with his guidepost on the Murray Valley Highway. Echuca FNC put up guideposts of all the players who played in the grand final. (Supplied: Katie Mills)

He had played two home-and-away games before being cleared by his doctors to return to football in time for the finals.

However, the Goulburn Valley Football League rejected Echuca's request for a special permit to allow him to play finals because he had not reached the required three-game minimum.

This year, Mills played enough games to qualify for finals and was named in Echuca's grand final side.

Murphy said the players were determined to win when they took to the field.

"There was no way they were going to lose it for AJ," he said.

A humble player

Mills's mother, Katie Mills said the scenes after the final siren were emotional, with players coming over to hug her and the family.

"It was obviously just a really emotional time, not only for him and us as his family, but the entire club," she told ABC Central Victoria Breakfast.

Ms Mills said he had managed to get through the entire season while receiving monthly chemotherapy.

"He's doing really, really well," she said.

"He's stable, no tumour progression at the moment, and that's literally best-case scenario."

She said he continued to have regular MRIs to monitor his condition.

AJ Mills played a practice match for Carlton's VFL side a week before he was diagnosed in 2025. (Supplied: Katie Mills)

Murphy said the players wanted to put Mills on their shoulders after the game, but Mills told them it was about everyone.

"That's the type of kid he is," Murphy said.

The senior premiership was part of a successful weekend for Echuca, with the reserves also winning their grand final.

The club's under-15 and under-17 netball sides also secured victories, giving Echuca four wins from five grand finals.

title: Producers lose equipment, livestock in central Queensland spring fires
text:
Just one week into spring, Kat Kirk was fighting to protect her livestock from a vicious bushfire.

The hobby farmer was struck by how quickly the blaze spread on her 15 hectare property in Port Curtis, just outside Rockhampton.

"I had five [or] six minutes between seeing it to trying to get everyone out," she said.

By the time fire crews were able to control it, Ms Kirk had lost a coop of breeding chickens and the blaze burnt all but half a hectare of her land.

"We barely just sort of got into the swing of spring and to see that coming over ... was very shocking," she said.

A coop of Kat Kirk's breeding hens could not be saved. (ABC Rural: Jessica D'Souza)

Ms Kirk was one of several producers in central Queensland caught off guard by the fires so early in the season.

Since September 1, multiple bushfires have occurred through the central Queensland region with the Queensland Fire Department issuing Watch and Act advice alerts for eight blazes.

The 2026 winter was Queensland's driest in six years, with rainfall across central Queensland well below average, according to the Bureau of Meteorology.

Rockhampton Rural Fire Service area manager Matthew Eckhardt said spring was usually busy, but the past few weeks had left his team "fatigued".

“We've had multiple crews out over multiple days going from one side of the community to the other [and] helping out," he said.

'We definitely weren't prepared'

Egg producer Debbie-Jo MacDonald, based 20 kilometres north of Ms Kirk, said while she was relieved her property was mostly spared from fire damage earlier this month, she was caught off guard.

"By the time we'd called Triple Zero (000), it had gone from a 5x5-metre fire to a 100x100-metre fire," she said.

"I think coming into this season and being so early in the season too, we definitely weren't prepared for the number of fires in our area."

Debbie Jo MacDonald plans to reinforce her property after the recent bushfire. (ABC Rural: Jessica D'Souza)

Ms MacDonald said her 800 chickens were unharmed during the fire and did not suffer with smoke inhalation in the days after.

"[During unplanned burns] there's always a lot of emotions going through your mind about. Have I done this? Have I looked after them well enough? Have we allowed them area to escape? Can they move? Can they survive on their own?"

Rebuild to cost thousands

At Gladstone, more than 100 kilometres south of Rockhampton, the main irrigation pump on Tony and Coleen McCray's vineyard was destroyed when multiple fires surrounded their property on September 3.

The blaze crossed the fire breaks, which are cleared strips of land designed to stop fire coming onto a property.

"We're going to be up for $50,000 … just to clear up all those dead trees and redo the fire breaks," Mr McCray said.

Tony and Coleen McCray lost their main irrigation pump during a fire on their vineyard. (Supplied: Tony McCray)

With dry conditions continuing in the region, the McCrays have concerns about the rest of spring and summer.

"Everything's very dry because [there has been] basically no rain since April," Mr McCray said.

" I really do believe that we are going to have a very long, dry summer. "

QFD urges producers to stay vigilant

Back at Ms Kirk's property, she is rebuilding and reinforcing in preparation for the months ahead.

Alex and Kat Kirk lost a coop of chickens and almost all their land was burnt in a bushfire in early spring. (ABC Rural: Jessica D'Souza)

"Our days haven't stopped until midnight," she said.

Tips for land owners: Have a fire plan

Be vigilant when working outdoors with machinery, and have another person nearby to ensure sparks do not accidentally start fires

Postpone hazard reduction burns until there is sufficient rain in your area

Call Triple Zero immediately if you see a fire on or near your property Source: Matthew Eckhardt, RFS Rockhampton manager

"We still look around the property and see a million things we've still got left to do … boundary fencing to fix and obviously so much clean-up left."

Nearby producers have donated supplies and volunteered to help.

"I've been in tears over all the support we've received from family and friends and complete strangers," she said.

Ms MacDonald is also reinforcing fire safety on her property, including building more water infrastructure.

"We're trying to prevent what could be a catastrophe and at least … take it back from a catastrophe to just an event," she said.

title: Younger Australians face a harder path to wealth, report shows
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Younger Australians face a future of working longer and struggling more to buy a home without the same early gains in income and wealth experienced by the generations before them.

The latest Intergenerational Report released on Monday by Treasurer Jim Chalmers has laid out how an aging population and falling birth rate would reshape Australia's economy in the next 40 years.

Fertility is expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065, which has sparked debate about what, if anything, could be done to persuade younger Australians to have more children.

The report, which is produced by Treasury every three years, found Australians born in the 1990s and after are better educated and likely to live and work longer, but the traditional path of accumulating wealth through home ownership has become harder.

The economy is expected to more than double in size in the next 40 years, with living standards continuing to rise, and the long-term budget outlook has had "significant" improvements since 2023.

But an older growing population, weaker productivity growth and rising costs in areas such as defence and health will put increasing pressure on government finances.

Handing down the report, Mr Chalmers said the global and generational risks faced by Australia were "serious" but argued the country was well-placed to deal with them.

"Australia's opportunities are endless," he said.

Jim Chalmers says Australia's future outlook has a fair amount of challenges and risks. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Birth rates spark baby bonus debate

Australia's declining fertility rate has prompted discussion about the return of financial incentives to encourage more people to have children.

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the government would not go into "promoting choices for individual families" but recognised Australians who did have children should be supported.

"That can be through our investments in early education and care, our three-day guarantee, our extending (paid parental leave) … ensuring that dads or second parents can take it, putting super on that so that people don't have that economic hit when they have children," she said.

Two growth solutions giving Labor a headache The two things holding up the economy are fast becoming the two most potent and dangerous political issues confronting the federal government.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan has called for greater support for families but said he did not think a revival of the "baby bonus" was the right way to encourage more Australians to have children.

"I think anything that we should do should be more … designed around the idea that if you … work for yourself, if you're helping yourself, we'll help you some more," he said.

" The baby bonus, it was just 'Here's some cash', without you having to put in the effort as well. "

Young Australians not achieving early wealth gains

The new report found fertility had fallen in Australia due to "complex economic, social and cultural factors" including more time in education, and career establishment, living with parents longer, as well as delayed partnership and childbearing.

Those demographic shifts have occurred as the economic fortunes of younger Australians have started to diverge from the generations before them.

Treasury said younger millennials were reaching their 30s without experiencing the early-career real disposable income increases compared with those born in the 1980s.

The average real household net worth rose from $0.5 million in 1993-94 to more than $1.3 million in 2019-20, but much of this wealth growth was concentrated among older households.

It is a trend that has been emerging for decades, with only about two-thirds of Australians born in the 1960s onwards doing better than their parents, compared with 80 per cent of people born in the 1950s.

Fewer home owners now

There would be about 250,000 more home owners aged between 25 and 34 if ownership rates had held up at 1981 levels.

House prices have risen about 400 per cent since 1999, which was more than twice as fast as the average income.

Australia is also building homes at roughly half the productivity of 30 years ago.

Home ownership rates among young people are lower than in the 1980s. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Treasury said population growth and smaller households have increased demand for housing, while weak construction and productivity has constrained the supply response.

The report also specifically identified investor tax concessions, like negative gearing and the 50 per cent capital gains tax (CGT) discount as contributing to the problem.

"These tax advantages have increased the share of housing owned by investors, at the expense of Australians looking to buy a home," it said.

Mr Chalmers said the government was changing arrangements for capital gains and negative gearing "to deal with plummeting home ownership rates among young people".

"To address one of the biggest drivers of intergenerational wealth inequality, we're reforming the tax system to reduce distortions in the housing market," he said.

Treasury noted between 80 to 90 per cent of investor housing lending since 2019 had gone towards the purchase of existing housing stock rather than new dwellings.

Australians to work for longer

Australia has more people participating in the workforce than Treasury expected thanks in large part to women working at increasing rates.

Female workforce participation is expected to continue rising until the mid-2040s, with the gap between men and women shrinking from 7.7 points now to a projected 5.4 points by 2065-66.

Older Australians are also working substantially more than previous generations, with participation among people aged over 65 rising 9.5 per cent since the 2002 Intergenerational Report.

Australians are projected to be working for longer. (Supplied)

Since 2023, an extra 1 per cent of Australians have continued to work beyond the age of 65, which the report has linked to the physical aspects of modern jobs and changes to retirement settings.

In his speech, Mr Chalmers said an aging population means a proportionately smaller workforce, and broader demand for health and aged care.

He said the number of Australians over 85 will triple by 2066, and a third of new healthcare spending over the next 40 years will be because of aging.

But he said Australia's workforce participation would continue growing while most OECD countries would see a decline.

Migration is also helping Australia maintain a workforce, with Treasury expecting the actual working-age population to continue growing due to overseas arrivals.

AI has potential to help economy grow

Despite worse demographics, Treasury now thinks Australia will spend less, run smaller deficits and carry substantially less debt than was forecast in 2023.

Looking at the budget long term, officials have projected Australia would run a surplus from 2029-30 for twenty years before aging and other pressures would push it back into deficit.

Health would remain a significant spending pressure, rising from 4 per cent to 6.2 per cent of GDP.

Public hospital funding is expected to account for more than 60 per cent of additional Commonwealth health spending.

AI is a risk to developing brains, neuroscientist warns Some young people are so worried about the impact artificial intelligence could have on their learning that they've decided to boycott it.

At the same time, Australia's transition to electric vehicles (EVs) is expected to have a significant impact on budget revenue as fewer motorists would pay the fuel excise charged on petrol and diesel.

The net fuel excise was projected to collapse to just 0.1 per cent of GDP by 2065-66, which is expected to drive the case for some form of EV road user charge to replace it.

Australia's productivity growth is expected to remain below its historical average, however Treasury said artificial intelligence (AI) presented a major opportunity to lift economic output.

AI is expected to be a significant force impacting Australia's economy in the next 40 years, but the potential benefit would depend on how effectively the country adopts and takes advantage of the technology.

title: Fremantle legend in tears as AFL grand final honour revealed
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Fremantle pioneer Shaun McManus will hand over the AFL premiership cup to captain Alex Pearce if the Dockers break through for their maiden flag.

Part of the inaugural 1995 Dockers squad, McManus has been named as Fremantle's cup presenter ahead of Saturday's grand final against back-to-back reigning premiers Brisbane.

The Lions are yet to name their presenter after three-time premiership player Jonathan Brown did so for last year's decider win over Geelong.

McManus was brought to tears when he was told he was the club's cup presenter during a segment on Perth radio this morning.

Peter Bell was named the club's presenter for the eventual 2013 grand final loss to Hawthorn.

Dockers chief Simon Garlick described McManus as a perfect embodiment of the club's values.

McManus began his AFL career as a 19-year-old, going on to play 228 games across 14 seasons.

He captained the team alongside Adrian Fletcher from 2000 to 2001, and played alongside current coach Justin Longmuir.

"Shaun perfectly sums up what a Fremantle person is," Garlick said in a club statement.

"He had a remarkable career as a Fremantle player, but beyond that he has been a champion of this club since our humble beginnings back in 1995.

"Those early foundation years weren't easy, and as a 19-year-old he came in, showed great qualities which resulted in him being named captain at just 24.

"The courage he showed on field speaks for itself, but ever since retiring he's been a passionate and positive influence, someone who purely lives and breathes Freo.

"If we are good enough to get the job done on Saturday, it will be a great moment to see Shaun present the cup to Alex, and his old teammate Justin."

McManus is the ninth-highest game record holder in the club's history and was the second behind Shane Parker to reach the 200-game milestone.

Retiring after the 2008 season, McManus remained at the club as a player development coach and transitioned through various off-field roles.

The 50-year-old became a Dockers life member in 2004.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

AAP

title: NRL set to act over 'embarrassing' referee abuse
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL has threatened to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

Footage from after full-time in Newcastle's 12-10 win over the Warriors at Eden Park showed a raft of bottles, cups and rubbish being thrown at Klein as he walked from the field.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

Klein had to be protected by security as fans abused the veteran referee and threw projectiles.

The NRL immediately launched an investigation into potential breaches of its spectators' code of conduct.

An integrity unit investigator had been at the ground.

"If found guilty, they [the fans] will be banned for a period of time from attending NRL games," ARL Commission chair Peter V'landys said.

Auckland police have since confirmed no arrests were made.

They said there were "no issues to note", other than two pitch invaders.

The Warriors exited the finals following the loss to the Knights. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Sunday's crowd of 48,511 marked the largest ever for a rugby league match in New Zealand, after the NRL made the call to move the match from Mount Smart Stadium.

The spectator abuse came after two contentious calls went against the Warriors late in the match, including a decision not to penalise Tyson Frizell for an escort in the dying minutes.

Warriors great Shaun Johnson hit out at the response of spectators after the match, labelling it "embarrassing".

"It leaves a bit of a sour taste in your mouth [after] what has been an unbelievable night with the colours, the energy, the happiness and celebration," Johnson said on Sky NZ's coverage.

"But there is just no need for it. It's just embarrassing.

"Ashley Klein has probably refereed the best game of rugby league I have seen in a long time tonight.

Hawks fans facing bans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

"He didn't take any gamesmanship in terms of people laying down. He didn't let people approach him whingeing.

"He didn't make the game about him. He let the players come and play and they dictated the outcome."

Warriors coach Andrew Webster vented his frustration in the post-match media conference, highlighting a bunker strip call on Te Maire Martin and the decision not to penalise Frizell for a possible escort on Leka Halasima.

"The last one, [when] two points would have drawn the game, he [Frizell] is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball, which they've told us you can't do," Webster said.

The incident came after AFL umpires also had bottles and cans thrown at them while leaving the MCG following Hawthorn's nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour and warned of minimum five-year bans for any fans found responsible.

AAP

title: Everything you need to know about the 2026 Brownlow Medal count
text:
The AFL's grand final week is here, and will begin as usual with the awarding of the Brownlow Medal tonight.

The best-and-fairest player of the 2026 season will be presented with the AFL's highest award at the end of the evening, with a first-time winner widely expected to be crowned.

The fashion on display beforehand on the red carpet will also be a big focus of attention.

Here is what you need to know about the AFL's night of nights.

What time is the 2026 Brownlow Medal?

The Brownlow Medal count will be held tonight, Monday, September 21, with the broadcast coverage starting at 7:30pm (AEST) and the count getting underway from 8pm.

Red carpet guests arrive from 5:15pm. The mark of the year winner will be announced at 8:35pm, and the goal of the year at 9pm.

How can I watch and follow the Brownlow Medal?

ABC Sport will be live blogging all the action with every vote from every round at abc.net.au.

The broadcast of the event from Melbourne's Crown Palladium will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus.

Who is the favourite to win the 2026 Brownlow?

Collingwood's Nick Daicos is the unbackable favourite.

As a demonstration of his favouritism, most bookmakers have listed him at $1.01 to win.

However, Daicos was also the strong favourite to win last season, before coming second to the Gold Coast's Matt Rowell by seven votes.

Other players in the discussion are Geelong's Bailey Smith, Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli and Carlton star Patrick Cripps.

Can umpires access stats when they give their votes?

Traditionally umpires haven't had access to game stats when they cast their votes directly after a match.

That has changed this year, after St Kilda's Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera was controversially deemed not the best player on the field in a game against Melbourne last season, despite being the clear star on the day.

This season umpires were given access to stats, including: kicks, handballs, disposals, marks, contested marks, tackles, goals, behinds, goal assists, score involvements, clearances, contested possessions, hitouts, kick-ins, intercept marks, intercept possessions and spoils.

Can the banned Sydney Swans players receive votes in the Brownlow?

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon were all banned from playing finals after breaching club standards.

The players were also deemed ineligible for the All Australian team, with Heeney and Warner both likely to have been named if not for the ban.

However, all players will be able to receive votes in the Brownlow, and all votes will count.

Heeney is considered a top 10 prospect in the award.

How does the Brownlow work?

Unlike other awards, the Brownlow Medal is decided by the votes of the umpires.

For every game of the home-and-away season (not counting finals), umpires award votes to the three best players on the field.

The best player is given three votes, the second-best two votes and the third-best one vote.

The votes are kept secret and are revealed round-by-round at the ceremony.

The player who ends with the most votes at the end of the season is crowned the Brownlow Medal winner.

The award is for the fairest and best players, so those who have been suspended for a week or more during the season are ineligible. Corey McKernan (1996) and Chris Grant (1997) are the most recent examples of ineligible players notching the most votes, while Jobe Watson won the medal in 2012 before having it rescinded in the wake of Essendon's supplements scandal.

In the event of a tie, the Brownlow can be shared, as was the case in 2003 when Adelaide's Mark Ricciuto, Collingwood's Nathan Buckley and Sydney's Adam Goodes shared the medal.

title: Investor saves Brisbane bowling club in $6m deal
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Coorparoo Bowls Club will no longer be demolished to make way for high-rise apartments, after the club was snapped up by a local investor for $6 million.

It comes after a multi-year-long campaign by the club's committee, which were due to be evicted in May this year.

Instead, the site was bought by Coorparoo local Will Griffin from Griffin Hospitality Group in a deal inked with Bowls Queensland.

As part of the deal, Griffin Hospitality will keep both of the bowling greens, one of which will be used for competitions and the other for casual players.

Coorparoo Bowls Club has been operating for 97 years. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Bowls Queensland chief executive Fletcher Dyson told 612 ABC Brisbane the organisation turned down much higher offers to ensure the bowling greens would remain.

"We turned a million dollars down to get this result," he said.

Mr Griffin said he planned to renovate the clubhouse, bar and kitchen, while keeping the feel and character of Coorparoo Bowls Club intact.

Both of the bowl greens will be maintained under the deal. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

"We see an enormous opportunity to give Coorparoo Bowls Club a bright new future while respecting everything that has made this venue so special for almost 100 years," Mr Griffin said.

"Our ambition is for people to be able to come to Coorparoo Bowls Club to play bowls, enjoy a meal, catch up with friends, bring the family, or simply be part of the community."

The existing Coorparoo Bowls Club committee, which campaigned to save the club, will continue to run it with a five-year lease.

Committee chairman Mark Delbridge said the deal was a triumph for the club members who fought to save the club.

"This is a really exciting new chapter for Coorparoo Bowls Club," he said.

title: Converse pulls sneaker ad critics say includes racist imagery
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan (KKK) and lynching.

The Instagram ad photo showed K-pop singer Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers.

The ad has since been removed by Converse. (Supplied: Converse)

Critics lashed out online, saying a white triangular image created by lighting on the skirt resembled a KKK hood and the way she held the sneakers made them look like the dangling feet of a lynching victim.

Converse, owned by Nike, issued a statement apologising and said it had removed the ad.

"We're sorry," the statement said.

"We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognise that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared.

" This should not have happened, and we will do better. "

Converse, based in Boston in the United States, declined to answer questions seeking additional information, including how the company screened ads before they were posted and how the ad was approved.

Karina and her management company, SM Entertainment Group, did not immediately respond to messages through their Instagram accounts.

Corporations 'failing the same test'

Retailers and top fashion brands have issued a string of apologies over the years for products and advertising criticised for being racially insensitive.

Last month, US retailer Target Corporation pulled a children's Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologising for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

The Converse photo sparked swift criticism, including calls to fire staff involved in the ad and boycott the company.

In a slew of social media comments, posters questioned how the ad could have cleared the company's advertising vetting process.

Other commenters defended Converse, saying they did not believe it was intentional.

Converse issued a statement saying the company understood why the image was "deeply upsetting". (AP Photo: Charles Krupa, file)

Civil rights attorney Lee Merritt, who is based in Texas, posted on Instagram that Converse's apology "doesn't undo what got past legal, marketing and leadership at every step".

"We keep having this conversation because corporations keep failing the same test," he wrote.

" Do better means catching this before it airs — not after we're offended. "

Converse, founded in Malden, Massachusetts, in 1908, makes the iconic Chuck Taylor All Star sneaker.

It was first released in 1917 as a non-skid basketball shoe and, in 1934, added Taylor's signature, after the basketball player promoted the sneaker, according to the company's website.

title: An ageing Australia must find ways to pay for world reshaped by AI, climate change
text:
Advertisement

Australia must rush to embrace artificial intelligence and the energy transition or “lag and languish”, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has declared, as he predicts sweeping changes over the next four decades driven by an ageing population. The 2026 Intergenerational Report, which gauges how economic and demographic trends will shape the nation and its finances over the next 40 years, flags four decades of continued deficits. This year’s Intergenerational Report flags a sharper decline in Australia’s fertility rate than previously predicted. Marija Ercegovac Australia’s population will also age more quickly and grow more slowly than previously expected due mostly to a lower number of births per woman. The population aged 85 and over is projected to treble to 1.9 million by 2066, putting additional pressure on the budget.

Advertisement

The report forecasts the federal budget be in deficit by 0.3 per cent of gross domestic product until 2036-37, which will then widen over the long term to reach 1.8 per cent of GDP in 2065-66. “This puts plainly the choice before us. Keep up and succeed, or lag and languish,” Chalmers said while unveiling his second Intergenerational Report since becoming treasurer. Gross federal debt as a share of GDP is projected to decline from 33.1 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to a low of 22.2 per cent of GDP in the mid-2050s. But this burden would grow to more than half the size of the economy, and deficits would blow out if not for relatively rosy productivity growth assumptions which have been challenged by some economists.

Advertisement

The opposition has described the IGR’s forecast of 1.2 per cent long-run productivity growth as an attempt by Treasurer Jim Chalmers to “cook the books”. Productivity has grown at an average of 0.8 per cent over the past 20 years. But the government has reverted from the 20-year average adopted in 2022 to the 30-year average of 1.2 per cent, even though Chalmers described the Morrison government’s use of a 20-year average as “rubbish”. Related Article Federal budget What six failed predictions taught Australia about its future Labor elder Bill Kelty has joined economists in urging Labor to reduce the burden on younger wage-earners by lowering income taxes and finding other ways to draw revenue. As revenue from the tobacco excise collapses, some economists and Coalition frontbencher Andrew Bragg have urged Labor to look at raising indirect taxes such as the GST. The report released on Monday states: “Without further reform, fiscal pressures from an ageing population and trends in the tax base will add to pressures on working-age Australians. Salary and wages are the largest source of taxable personal income. Indirect taxes are projected to keep declining, which will increase the share of tax receipts from personal income taxes.” The report identifies four “transformations” that will intensify in coming decades and have profound implications for Australia’s economy and society. These are:

Advertisement

Artificial intelligence The report says the economic and social implications of AI for Australia are “profound”, although this will depend on the evolution of the technology and how broadly AI is adopted. Australia is well positioned to benefit from the global AI revolution, given our stable institutions, abundant renewable energy potential and well-developed international connectivity, including in the Indo-Pacific region. Geopolitical fragmentation Conflict and competition between countries is intensifying, the report warns. Economic relationships will increasingly be shaped by security and strategic alignment – not just the efficiency of production. “Economic openness will continue to deliver growth, put downward pressure on inflation and drive productivity in Australia, but countries and companies will need to balance supply chain efficiency with national security and resilience,” the report said.

Advertisement

The energy transition The shift to renewable energy will be more important and urgent as global energy supply chains

face disruption. But households will benefit from cheaper electricity as the transition matures. “The energy transition will become even more urgent in the context of competition and conflict, and the increased importance of energy security,” the report said. Ageing and the care economy As the population ages, increased demand for care and support services will reinforce shifts in the economy towards services. This long-run trend towards services and the care economy will coincide with the adoption and diffusion of AI and broader changes in the industrial base.

Advertisement

“The long-run shift towards services is expected to continue, with growth in household services and the care economy underpinned by population ageing and rising incomes,” the report said. Related Article Australian economy Jim Chalmers flags fresh tax cuts, warns of ‘confronting’ news in economic outlook The intergenerational report predicts Australians will be wealthier, live longer and remain healthier over the next 40 years. Real gross national income per person – the average amount earned by each Australian domestically and overseas – is projected to increase by 55 per cent by 2066. However, the average annual growth rate in national income per person is projected to slow to 1.1 per cent over the next 40 years, compared to 1.9 per cent over the past 40 years. Life expectancy for women is forecast to reach 89.5 years and 86.1 years for men by 2065-66 supported by ongoing improvements in health care, healthy lifestyles and medical innovation.

Advertisement

Population growth is expected to grow at 0.9 per cent per year over the next 40 years, down from 1.4 per cent over the past 40 years, primarily driven by a lower fertility rate. The total fertility rate – the number of expected births per woman – is expected to fall from its current level of 1.48 to 1.34 children per woman by 2065-66 The population is projected to grow from 28 million today to 39.3 million by 2065-66. Deaths are projected to outnumber births by the 2060s as Australia ages, the first time this has been forecast in Australia. title: Larvotto rolls out first concentrate from NSW antimony-gold mine
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Larvotto rolls out first concentrate from NSW antimony-gold mine Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS September 21, 2026 — 1:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In kicking off antimony-gold concentrate production from its freshly refurbished Hillgrove mining operation in New South Wales, Larvotto Resources has officially joined the ranks of Australian producers. The company says it has successfully commissioned the processing plant’s flotation circuit and concentrate filter presses, allowing it to produce its first saleable product just a month after restarting operations. The milestone clears the way for Larvotto to begin delivering into binding offtake agreements it has already secured with commodity trading giants Wogen Resources for its antimony and Glencore International AG for its gold. Larvotto Resources’ Jameson cleaner cell removing impurities from its first antimony-gold concentrate at the company’s processing plant at Hillgrove in New South Wales. Over its planned initial eight-year mine life, Hillgrove is forecast to produce 4900 tonnes of antimony and 40,500 ounces of gold per annum. The antimony concentrate, cleaned to a 60 per cent product specification, is covered by a binding seven-year offtake agreement with Wogen Resources. The deal gives Wogen exclusive global sales rights for all antimony produced from Hillgrove during the period. Larvotto says Wogen representatives travelled from the UK to witness the company’s first concentrate production, a solid vote of confidence in the newly commissioned operation.

Advertisement

‘Achieving first concentrate reinforces Hillgrove’s position as a globally significant new source of antimony.’ Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks A separate binding agreement will see all gold concentrate produced during the first seven years of mining sold to Glencore, covering an expected annual offtake of about 15,000 dry metric tonnes of concentrate. It’s also worth noting that Larvotto is using a gravity gold separation circuit at the front end of the mill. However, rather than relying on classic low-gravity gold recovery devices like simple spiral arrays or jigs, the modernised Hillgrove flow sheet relies strictly on centrifugal and multi-gravity units to intercept the gold before it enters the flotation circuits. The primary workhorse of the gravity circuit is a Knelson concentrator, which sits within the grinding and milling circuit. As the primary ball mill reduces the ore size down to the target micron-size range, the pulp passes through the centrifugal Knelson unit. The company’s employment of a gravity circuit means a portion of its estimated 40,500 ounces of gold per year will likely be recovered as doré bars directly on-site.

Advertisement

Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “With the successful production of first concentrate, we now move into the delivery phase of the offtake agreements we have secured, namely the antimony offtake with Wogen Resources and the gold concentrate offtake with Glencore. These partnerships are significant, providing Larvotto with established access to global commodity markets and supply chains.” The Hillgrove project, 23 kilometres east of Armidale in northern NSW, already hosts a significant resource of 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent at an impressive grade of 7.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent, ranking it among the world’s top ten antimony deposits and the biggest in Australia. Despite this red letter moment in Hillgrove’s development, the company is not resting on its laurels. It has already defined a significant exploration target for the new Midas lode, along strike from existing workings near the plant site, with a preferred midpoint estimate of 3.95 million tonnes at 5.16 g/t gold equivalent, for 656,000 ounces of gold. The broader conceptual range reported for Midas spans from 2.7Mt to 10.7Mt, containing between 223,000 and 2.95 million ounces of gold equivalent. Recent drilling at the Midas zone returned a spectacular hit of 8 metres at 16.11 g/t gold equivalent, the highest-grade gold-antimony intersection ever recorded for the zone. The standout result came from a diamond hole which bored through 8m assaying 16.11g/t gold equivalent from 301m, including 4.5m at 27.78g/t gold equivalent from 302.5m depth. The company says that potential also exists for a third payable metal at Hillgrove, with drilling at the Blacklode prospect intercepting a remarkable 0.4m grading 9.09 per cent tungsten trioxide. Larvotto has already defined an initial tungsten mineral resource of 4,774 tonnes of tungsten trioxide.

Advertisement

Historically, tungsten mineralisation has never been estimated as part of the Hillgrove mineral resources. But once the company completes its studies on the scale and mineability potential of its tungsten resources, it could soon find itself producing a second critical industrial metal, alongside antimony. The Hillgrove process plant already features an entirely independent, pre-existing tungsten gravity circuit. While it sits separately from the main gold-antimony recovery circuits, Larvotto aims to map out and re-integrate the tungsten infrastructure to exploit its tungsten stream as its antimony-gold production scales up. Larvotto’s restart of its Hillside operation seems impeccably timed. Antimony is a designated critical mineral in Australia, the US and Europe, and market watchers point to tightening geopolitical tensions and a push to secure supply chains outside of China. At the same time, gold has held above A$6000 per ounce this year, providing a strong tailwind for any new producer hitting the market. Making the leap from explorer to producer is notoriously difficult; however, Larvotto appears to have navigated it with aplomb. With a fully funded operation, potentially three important commodities, and two product offtakes already locked in with global players, the company is now shifting its focus from building a mine to running one. And with a suite of surrounding nearby exploration targets screaming for the drill bit, that initial eight-year mine life might just be the start of the story. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has taken legal action against former Super Retail Group chief executive Anthony Heraghty, alleging he breached his directors’ duties and provided misleading information to the board and financial market concerning his relationship with the group’s former head of human resources. ASIC alleges Heraghty, who was recently hired by appliance group Winnings for an expected float on the ASX, failed to disclose and manage conflicts of interest arising from an alleged undisclosed relationship he had with a senior executive at the company. Dan Peled “ASIC alleges Mr Heraghty put himself in a position where his personal interests conflicted with his duties to Super Retail Group and that he failed to properly disclose and manage that conflict,” ASIC chair Sarah Court said. “The allegations in this matter raise important issues about governance, transparency and trust in the information provided to boards and the market.”

ASIC alleges Heraghty continued to supervise Jane Kelly, the HR boss, and took part in decisions affecting her employment, remuneration, incentives, rewards and redundancy package. He also allegedly participated in board and committee discussions of complaints and anticipated legal proceedings concerning the alleged undisclosed relationship. “This case is not about private relationships, but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders,” Court said. In 2024, Super Retail’s former chief legal officer Rebecca Farrell and former company secretary Amelia Berczelly launched separate legal actions against their previous employer for allegedly punishing them for trying to bring to light allegations about Heraghty having a relationship with Kelly and the alleged inappropriate use of company funds to further the relationship. The legal battle ultimately cost Super Retail $40 million, according to disclosures in its financial accounts. Heraghty also allegedly provided or authorised information to be released to SRG’s board and the market that omitted information concerning the alleged undisclosed relationship and was therefore misleading, ASIC said.

title: German chancellor declares AfD state election win 'a disaster'
text:
In brief The far-right AfD secured its latest state-level election win in eastern Germany.

The result puts fresh pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as his party suffers a historic setback.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won state elections in north-east Germany, delivering the worst result for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party since 1949.

"It's a disaster," Merz said after exit polls were published on Monday, but signalled he would fight on as chancellor and continue his reform agenda, despite speculation that a bad result could prompt him to resign.

The AfD was set to win 37 per cent in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) on 35.5 per cent and far in front of Merz’s conservatives, who got 5.5 per cent and barely crossed the threshold to enter the state parliament, according to exit polls on ARD public television.

Sunday's result looks set to deliver another first-place finish at the state level in a month for the AfD party, which tops national opinion polls but has been kept out of power by the other main parties' refusal to work with it.

In another election in the capital, Berlin, which also took place on Sunday, the far-left Die Linke party was at 24.5 per cent, while Merz's conservatives were at 20 per cent.

The AfD also gained in strength in the liberal city, hitting 16 per cent. It is the first time the Linke topped polls in the state, where it wants to nationalise housing from corporate landlords and cap rents.

The elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural state in the formerly communist east, and in the capital, Berlin, follow the 6 September election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD came close to the rare feat of winning an absolute majority.

Elections in the two states would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD's success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shock waves through Europe.

In just over a decade, the party, which wants to take tough action to deport foreigners with no right to stay in Germany, restore energy ties with Russia, and quit the euro, has transformed itself from a fringe eurosceptic movement into the country's most popular party.

The exit polls underscore the advances the AfD has made in recent years and raise fresh questions over the "firewall" strategy, under which the other main parties refuse to enter coalition agreements with it.

Merz has struggled

Elected last year on a promise of reforms to return Germany's stagnant economy to growth, Merz has struggled to win over voters, compounding resentment over unpopular pension, tax and healthcare reforms with a stream of communication missteps.

Disillusion with his government has hung over the campaigns in both Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, where voters have focused on issues including soaring energy and housing costs. Merz presented a consumer relief package on Friday that included tax cuts on gas and diesel.

Several people who voted in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania said living costs were a major concern.

"Here in Schwerin, with these wages, you can hardly afford anything anymore," voter Carlotta Heick told Reuters in the state capital.

One elderly man criticised funding for foreign aid.

"We need our money here, for our country, for children and pensioners," he said, asking not to give his name.

title: Motor neurone disease rates are rising. This new clinic hopes to stop it at the start
text:
In Brief The Brain Institute and Clinic will bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease.

MND impacts the brain and neurons that control muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.

As the rates of a once-rare neurological disease rise, it is hoped that Australia's first combined institute and clinic focused on brain diseases will help find an effective treatment.

On Monday, Macquarie University will launch its Brain Institute and Clinic to bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease (MND) to understand its origins and how to treat it.

MND impacts parts of a person's brain and neurons that control their muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.

It can affect adults of any age and most cases are not genetic.

Macquarie University deputy vice-chancellor Patrick McNeil noted there was still no effective cure for the deadly disease, despite it becoming increasingly common.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The purpose of the institute was to find treatments and deliver them to patients more quickly, he said.

"It typically takes an average of 17 years between when an important research discovery is made ... and when that is implemented in the clinic," McNeill told the Australian Associated Press.

"When you have integrated research and clinical institutions, that journey is shortened."

READ MORE I was researching motor neurone disease, then I was diagnosed with it myself

Earlier this month, NSW became the first jurisdiction in the world to make MND notifiable, meaning medical professionals are now legally required to report cases to the government.

McNeil said he hoped the decision would help researchers better understand the cause.

"It would be good if the other states follow because that is the way that you can find if there is an environmental agent," he said.

"Because what we have been seeing anecdotally is these clusters of cases that seem to be more frequent in a particular town or region than you would expect."

Dominic Rowe, who heads up Macquarie's Neurology Clinic, said 800 Australians would die from the disease this year.

"But I actually disagree with using the term die; motor neuron disease kills you," he said.

"We need to redouble our efforts into working out why so we can fix it."

The facility will also do research and treatment around Parkinson's disease and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease.

READ MORE Want to reduce your dementia risk? Lifestyle changes are only part of the picture

Macquarie University professor James Burrell said he was hopeful experts could build on recent breakthroughs in dementia treatment.

He said there were therapies available that slowed the physical progression of dementia caused by Alzheimer's.

"We now have disease-modifying therapies for this disease, and this gives me tremendous hope that we can identify disease-modifying therapies for other neurodegenerative diseases as well," Burrell said.

title: China's 13-year-old swimming prodigy Yu Zidi makes waves at Asian Games
text:
In brief 13-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi was fastest in the women's 200m butterfly heats.

The first gold medal of the 20th Asian Games was won on Sunday by host nation Japan's triathlete, Takumi Hojo.

A 13-year-old swimmer from China has kicked off the 20th Asian Games in blistering form.

Yu Zidi, who does not turn 14 until next month, was fastest by far in the women's 200m butterfly heats.

The Games, being held in Japan, were officially declared open on Saturday by Japan's Emperor Naruhito although there were a large number of empty seats at the 30,000-capacity stadium in Nagoya.

It sounded the starting pistol on two weeks of intense action as the continent's finest athletes compete in more than 40 sports before the curtain comes down on October 4. title: Why Pauline Hanson joined forces with Muslim and Vietnamese-born MPs
text:
In brief Pauline Hanson, Fatima Payman and Dai Le have united to argue parliamentary staffing allocations are unfair.

The prime minister has significant discretion over personal staff, but the trio wants an independent system instead.

Pauline Hanson and Fatima Payman have clashed over race, religion and politics.

But this week, the One Nation leader and Muslim independent senator stood together, alongside Vietnamese-born independent MP Dai Le.

At the centre of their unlikely alliance is a fight over parliamentary staffing, with the three accusing Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of unfairly determining who gets additional staff and calling for the system to be taken out of the prime minister's hands.

The unlikely trio appeared together at Parliament House on Thursday, arguing the way personal staff are allocated to politicians is unfair and lacks transparency.

Their grievance centres on an unusual feature of Australia's parliamentary system: while MPs and senators employ their own staff, the prime minister has significant discretion over the allocation of additional personal staff.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

That discretion has previously faced scrutiny in parliament.

Why did Hanson, Payman and Le join forces?

Despite their political differences, all three say they are being denied the staffing resources they need to do their jobs adequately.

Payman, who left Labor in 2024 after crossing the Senate floor over Palestinian statehood, currently has no additional personal staff allocated to her.

Le, who defeated Labor to win the western Sydney seat of Fowler as an independent in 2022, has one.

One Nation, meanwhile, increased its representation at the 2025 election but says its staffing allocation did not increase accordingly.

According to the Australian Associated Press, modelling puts One Nation's allocation at 0.83 personal staff per parliamentarian, compared with 4.09 for Labor and 1.47 for the Coalition.

READ MORE Political leaders condemn Pauline Hanson over resurfaced remarks about Indigenous culture

Those figures include different categories of parliamentarians and office-holders, so they are not a direct like-for-like comparison of backbench MPs.

Hanson, Payman and Le argue the differences demonstrate the need for a more transparent and independent system.

According to The Conversation, Le told reporters on Thursday there were "no published criteria, no explanation, no appeal" for staffing decisions.

The three have threatened to pursue legislative changes when parliament returns in October to remove the prime minister's power over non-government personal staff allocations and give the responsibility to an independent authority.

Who actually decides how many staff politicians get?

Parliamentary staffing is divided into different categories, with different rules governing how positions are allocated.

Politicians generally have two broad categories of staff: electoral staff and personal staff.

Electorate staff perform work such as assisting constituents and supporting MPs and senators in their parliamentary duties.

Personal staff can perform different roles, including providing policy advice, research, communications and support for a parliamentarian's work in Canberra.

They are employed under the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act, commonly known as the MOP(S) Act, and cannot legally be employed for party-political purposes.

But additional personal staff are not distributed to every politician according to a single automatic formula.

The Department of Finance says the prime minister determines the number of personal employee positions allocated to ministers and assistant ministers, as well as the allocation given to the Opposition.

The prime minister also determines the allocation given to the leader of a minority party, who can then distribute those positions among their party's MPs, and may allocate personal staff to independent parliamentarians.

That means gaining another MP or senator does not necessarily translate into an increase in personal staff members.

Albanese's power over staff members is not unique. The system has given successive prime ministers significant control over personal staffing allocations

Why do extra staff matter?

Additional personal staff provide support across a range of parliamentary duties, and can affect their capacity to carry out parliamentary and electorate work.

They can research legislation, prepare MPs and senators for parliamentary debates and committee hearings, develop policy advice, deal with media and stakeholders and help offices manage correspondence and constituent issues.

Crossbenchers and smaller parties also have fewer parliamentary colleagues and party resources to draw on than the major parties.

READ MORE Dai Le thought she would die on her journey to Australia. She wants it to be easier for others to get here

The Parliamentary Library has previously noted that staffing levels for crossbenchers have varied significantly over time, and have sometimes changed depending on the political circumstances of the parliament.

When independents held the balance of power following the 2010 election, for example, additional staff were allocated to crossbench MPs. Those arrangements changed after the 2013 election.

Additional personal staff can assist parliamentarians with work including scrutinising legislation, preparing for parliamentary debates and participating in committee work.

Has this fight happened before?

The allocation of personal staff to crossbench parliamentarians has previously been contested, including since the Albanese government took office in 2022.

After Labor took office four years ago, Albanese reduced the number of additional personal staff allocated to crossbench parliamentarians, prompting significant criticism from independents.

A Parliamentary Library research paper subsequently noted that while the overall number of personal staff had increased substantially over the longer term, allocations to crossbenchers and former leaders had not increased in the same way.

The issue returned to parliament in 2025, when senators sought to change how personal staff were allocated to non-government parliamentarians and reduce the prime minister's discretion over the process.

A bill co-sponsored by Coalition and crossbench senators, including Hanson and Payman, proposed guaranteeing minimum personal staffing levels for non-government parliamentarians.

It also sought to limit the prime minister's discretion over those minimum allocations.

The bill passed its second reading in the Senate but was ultimately defeated at the third-reading stage in September 2025.

The Senate nevertheless backed an amendment calling for the government to work with elected groups and independents to develop a "fair and independent staffing model" that accounted for representation, staff wellbeing and workloads.

Reviews of parliamentary workplaces have also previously recommended greater transparency around staffing allocations and an evidence-based examination of workloads.

Why is their alliance so unusual?

Hanson and Payman, in particular, have a long history of clashing politically.

In 2024, Hanson sought to have Payman's eligibility to sit in parliament investigated over questions surrounding her Afghan citizenship.

Payman responded with a fierce attack on Hanson in the Senate, comments she was subsequently required to withdraw.

The political tensions between them remained.

Payman told reporters on Thursday, however, that politicians should be able to set those disagreements aside when they find a common cause, according to The Guardian.

title: Australia wants a seat at the UN's most powerful table. What power would it yield?
text:
IN BRIEF Australia is campaigning for a seat on the UN body responsible for international peace and security.

A seat would give Australia a vote and role in key negotiations, but not the veto held by five permanent members.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is heading to New York with a diplomatic pitch that has been more than a decade in the making: Putting Australia back on the United Nations Security Council.

Australia is campaigning for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2029-30, which would mark its first stint on the powerful UN body since 2014.

The government says a seat would give Australia a stronger voice on decisions affecting the country and the region.

Australia's campaign is expected to focus on issues including artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety, as well as climate action, international law and support for Pacific nations.

But what exactly does the UN Security Council do, and what would Australia gain by being on it?

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is the UN Security Council?

The Security Council is one of the six main bodies of the United Nations and has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.

It is made up of 15 countries, each with one vote.

Five of them — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — are permanent members, while another 10 countries are elected by the UN General Assembly to serve two-year terms.

Unlike most other UN bodies, the Security Council can make decisions that member states are obligated to implement.

READ MORE We came to meet Tim Cook, but left with just a few photos

It can impose sanctions, establish peacekeeping operations and, in some circumstances, authorise the use of force. It can also investigate disputes, call for peaceful settlements and make recommendations aimed at maintaining or restoring international peace and security.

For a substantive resolution to pass, it needs at least nine votes.

And there is an important catch — each of the five permanent members has veto power, meaning a negative vote from any one of them can block a substantive resolution even if it otherwise has enough support.

Australia would not gain that veto power if elected, as it belongs exclusively to the five permanent members of the Security Council.

Non-permanent members such as Australia have the same single vote on council decisions, but cannot unilaterally block a substantive resolution.

What would Australia gain?

While a non-permanent seat does not come with a veto, it gives countries a direct role in decisions they would otherwise largely have to influence from outside the council.

Australia would have a vote on Security Council decisions and be involved in negotiating resolutions and other outcomes on conflicts and security crises around the world.

It would also take part in closed meetings and consultations between council members and could chair subsidiary bodies, including sanctions committees.

Every member also takes a turn holding the presidency of the Security Council for one calendar month, allowing them to preside over meetings and help shape the council's program of work.

Australia's previous term shows the practical difference membership can make.

During 2013-14, Australia participated in hundreds of council meetings, including closed meetings available only to members, and was closely involved in negotiating dozens of resolutions and presidential statements.

Its seat became particularly significant following the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014, which killed 298 people, including 38 Australian citizens and residents.

Australia authored and led negotiations on Security Council Resolution 2166, which was unanimously adopted four days after the crash.

The resolution condemned the downing of the plane, called for a full and independent investigation and demanded access to the crash site.

Australia also used its term to work on humanitarian access in Syria, counter-terrorism, small arms and the protection of civilians.

Why does Australia want a seat again?

The government argues that Australia's security and prosperity depend on an international system in which countries follow agreed rules and work collectively on global problems.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said a seat would give Australia "a stronger voice in the decisions that affect us and our region", describing the country as an active middle power with a role to play in international peace and security.

The bid is also increasingly focused on what Australia argues will be emerging security challenges by the time it takes up the seat.

Technology is expected to be central to the campaign, with the government arguing that artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety will increasingly intersect with international peace and security.

Speaking at a Security Council debate last year, Wong said AI had the potential to transform conflict and diplomacy and argued the council should play a role in developing international rules and norms around its use.

She said Australia's experience in digital infrastructure and technology partnerships would form part of what it could bring to the council.

Australia's broader foreign policy priorities, including the Pacific, climate change, protecting civilians and supporting international law, are also expected to feature in the campaign.

How does Australia get elected?

Australia cannot simply nominate itself and take a seat.

The 10 non-permanent positions are distributed between regional groupings, with five seats coming up for election each year.

Australia belongs to the Western European and Others Group, or WEOG, and is seeking one of the group's two seats available for the 2029-30 term.

So far, Australia and Finland are the only candidates for those two positions, meaning the positions are currently uncontested.

But Australia must still win the support of two-thirds of UN General Assembly members present and voting when the election is held in June 2028.

If all 193 UN member states were present and voted, that would mean securing around 129 votes.

It helps explain why the government is campaigning years before Australia would actually take its seat.

The bid itself is not new. It was first announced in 2015 under the former Coalition government, following Australia's previous stint on the council.

Australia has served five terms on the Security Council since the UN was established, most recently in 2013-14.

A sixth term would not give Australia the power enjoyed by the council's five permanent members.

But for two years, it would give Australia something it otherwise does not have: a seat, a vote and a direct role in negotiations at the UN body responsible for some of the world's most consequential decisions on peace and security.

title: John Farnham to skip tribute concert amid worsening health, family says
text:
In brief Australian and international music stars are due to perform at a John Farnham tribute concert.

Farnham would have loved to attend a tribute concert in his honour, his family says.

John Farnham's tribute concert will go ahead without him as the Australian music legend's family reveals his health has deteriorated.

The music-industry giant will be honoured by local and international performing greats at a blockbuster charity gig at Melbourne's Rod Laver Arena on Sunday, raising funds for the cancer support services that helped him through his own battle with the disease.

title: We came to the Apple mothership to meet Tim Cook, but left with just a few photos and a silent movie
text:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spent an hour on Sunday (AEST) with former Apple chief Tim Cook at the company's mothership, doing a walk and talk through the famed infinite circle gardens in the heart of Silicon Valley and getting a demonstration of the tech juggernaut’s new parental controls.

Apple’s strict management of media access meant there was no invitation for Australian press cameras to capture the moment Albanese says he was lauded by the director of Apple’s board and credited with driving international efforts to keep kids off social media.

Just a handful of still photographs and a 27-second compilation of silent video were cleared and circulated by the Prime Minister’s Office, showing his interactions with the cult figure, who has a devoted following in the tech world.

Even during a demonstration of the products and controls for Aussie journalists, the company’s media minders asked us not to show the faces of Apple employees, record audio, or publish any further pictures of the inside of the building.

The whole experience aligned with Apple’s famously protective approach to independent media roaming its facilities and its wish to impose privacy measures on its internal workings, from the architecture to the acoustics.

With this high-profile tête-à-tête now Instagram official, Albanese moves on to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, drumming up support for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council.

In no small part, his government's digital policies will propel this bid, including restrictions on social media companies to protect children from online harm.
